definition: Pay for each hour worked, usually paid weekly.
A fixed amount of pay per year, usually paid monthly.
note: Divide by 12 for monthly pay, by 52 for weekly pay.

definition: Pay for each item made: number of items × rate per item.
Pay calculated as a percentage of the value of sales.
A fixed basic amount paid in addition to commission.
Hours worked beyond the normal week, paid at a higher rate.
note: Time-and-a-half is \(1.5\times\) the hourly rate; apply it only to the extra hours.

definition: Overtime paid at \(1.5\times\) the normal hourly rate.
Overtime paid at \(2\times\) the normal hourly rate.
Total earnings before any deductions.
Earnings after deductions: gross income − deductions.
Amounts taken off gross pay, e.g. income tax, pension, insurance.
Tax charged on earnings, often worked out from a tax table.
A range of income taxed at one rate; each rate applies only to the part of income inside its band.
note: Do not apply the top rate to the whole income.

definition: Income that is not taxed; tax is charged only on income above it.
note: Subtract the allowance before applying the tax rate.

definition: Income on which tax is charged (after allowances).
Money paid for borrowing, or earned from investing, money.
Interest on the original principal only: \(I=\frac{PRT}{100}\).
Interest added each period that then earns interest: \(V=P\left(1+\frac{r}{100}\right)^n\).
The amount of money originally invested or borrowed.
The percentage charged or earned per period, usually per year.
For each year; an interest rate per annum is a yearly rate.
note: Convert months to years (\(\div12\)) before using \(T\).

definition: Buying by paying a deposit, then equal instalments; usually costs more than the cash price.
The first payment made when buying on hire purchase.
One of the equal regular payments made after the deposit.
The price if paid in full at once.
The number to multiply by for a percentage change, e.g. 1.05 for +5%, 0.85 for −15%.
Repeated increase by the same rate: \(y=a(1+r)^n\) (r as a decimal).
Repeated decrease by the same rate: \(y=a(1-r)^n\) (r as a decimal).
A fall in value over time, usually by a fixed percentage per year.
A rise in value over time.
The price a trader pays for an item.
The price at which an item is sold.
Selling price − cost price (when positive).
Cost price − selling price (when selling for less than cost).
Profit as a percentage of the cost price: \(\frac{\text{profit}}{\text{cost price}}\times100\).
note: Divide by the cost price, not the selling price.

definition: The amount or percentage added to the cost price to get the selling price.
A reduction from the original price.
note: Percentage discount uses the original price as 100%.

definition: Tax added to a price: price with tax = price × \(\left(1+\frac{r}{100}\right)\).
note: To remove tax, divide by \(1+\frac{r}{100}\); do not subtract \(r\%\).

definition: Finding the original amount from a value after a percentage change, by dividing by the multiplier.
Work out from given facts or figures, showing working.
Give every step leading to the given result; the answer alone earns nothing.
Give a sensible approximate value, usually by rounding first or using a model.

term: give your answer correct to 3 s.f.
definition: Round only the final answer to 3 significant figures; keep full values in working.
Use the previous answer or result to do this part.
Give reasons or say why/how in words, supported by evidence from the context.
Give the answer without significant working, only if it follows directly.
Calculate from given facts or figures (with or without a calculator), showing enough working for method marks.
Rate per year; time must be in years.
note: Using months as \(T\): 18 months is \(T=1.5\), not 18.

definition: Simple: interest on \(P\) only; compound: interest on the growing total.
note: Using \(PRT/100\) for a compound question, or \(1.05^n\) for a simple one.

definition: For \(r\%\) growth use \(1+\frac{r}{100}\).
Simple interest on the outstanding balance for the whole loan period.
note: Charging the rate on the cash price instead of the balance after the deposit.

definition: Decay: multiply by \(1-r\) each year.
note: Subtracting \(n\times r\%\) of the original value (simple) instead of compounding.

definition: The amount still owed after the deposit: cash price − deposit.
note: Forgetting to subtract the deposit first.

definition: Find the smallest whole number of years where the value is below the target.
note: Giving a non-integer \(n\), or the year before the value drops below.

definition: Interest = final value − principal.
note: Forgetting to subtract \(P\) when the question asks for interest.

definition: Keep full calculator values until the final answer.
note: Rounding intermediate values, which changes the final answer.

definition: An action with an uncertain result, such as rolling a die.
One possible result of an experiment.
A set of one or more outcomes of an experiment.
The list or table of all possible outcomes of an experiment (also called the possibility space).
Outcomes that all have the same probability, for example when an object is chosen at random.
The event that A does not happen, written A′; P(A′) = 1 − P(A).
A set of events is exhaustive if it contains every possible outcome, so one of them must happen.
One repeat of an experiment.
The proportion of trials in which an event happens; an estimate of its probability.
The number of times an event is expected in n trials: n × P(A).
Events that cannot both happen: they have no outcomes in common, so P(A ∩ B) = 0.
P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B); for mutually exclusive events, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B).
A diagram that shows events as circles inside a rectangle of all outcomes.
A ∪ B: A or B or both.
A ∩ B: both A and B.
The set with no elements, written ∅.
Neither A nor B: (A ∪ B)′, with probability 1 − P(A ∪ B).
In probability, A or B means A or B or both, not “exactly one”.
Adding P(A) and P(B) for overlapping events counts A ∩ B twice; subtract P(A ∩ B) once.
With two ordinary six-sided dice, (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different outcomes; the sample space has 36 outcomes, not 21.
n × P(A) need not be a whole number and is not a guaranteed result.
A random variable that can take any value in an interval, such as a time or a mass.
A function f with f(x) ≥ 0 and total area 1 under its graph; areas under it give probabilities. Short form: PDF.
The height of a PDF or of a histogram scaled so that its total area is 1; it is not a probability and can be more than 1.
A constant, often k, chosen so that the total area under a PDF is 1.
For a PDF, the area under the graph between a and b is P(a < X < b).
f(x) can be greater than 1; only areas under the graph are probabilities.
For a continuous random variable a single value has probability 0, so < and ≤ give the same answer.
A function with total area 1 is not a PDF if it is negative anywhere in its range.
Integrate only where f(x) is non-zero; outside its range f(x) = 0.
The angle at the centre of a circle subtended by an arc equal in length to the radius. 2π radians = 360°.
An arc or line subtends an angle at a point when its two ends are joined to that point to form the angle.
Part of the circumference of a circle.
A unit of angle in which a full turn is 360°. To change to radians multiply by π/180.
Give an exact answer written as a multiple of π, such as 5π/12, not a decimal.
In angle work π stands for π radians, which is 180°; it is not 3.14 degrees.
Use radian mode for sin, cos or tan of an angle in radians; degree mode gives wrong values.
Degrees to radians multiply by π/180 (the number gets smaller); radians to degrees multiply by 180/π.
Integration seen as undoing differentiation: find a function whose derivative is the one given.
A function such as e^x or e^(ax+b); its derivative is a multiple of itself.
Integrating f(ax+b) by integrating f and dividing by a, the coefficient of x (a must not be 0; for 1/(ax+b), ax+b must not be 0 on the interval).
An integral with no limits; the answer is a family of functions written with + c.
The arbitrary constant c added to an indefinite integral, because constants differentiate to zero.
The logarithm to base e, written ln. Its derivative is 1/x for x > 0.
The size of a number without its sign, written |x|. Used in ln|ax+b| so the result works when ax+b < 0.
An integral with limits, giving a number: F(upper limit) minus F(lower limit).
The integral of e^(ax+b) is (1/a)e^(ax+b) + c for a not 0; do not multiply by a.
The power rule fails for x^(-1) because it would divide by zero; use ln instead.
ln is undefined for negatives; use ln|ax+b| when the limits make ax+b negative, and never integrate across the point where ax+b = 0.
To differentiate uv: u times the derivative of v, plus v times the derivative of u.
Two functions multiplied together, such as x² times (3x − 1)⁴.
Finding a derivative from the definition: the limit of δy/δx as δx tends to 0.
The slope of the tangent to a curve at a point; equal to dy/dx there.
note: In A Level work the gradient at a point comes from the derivative.

definition: A point on a curve where the gradient dy/dx is 0.
note: Also called a turning point when it is a maximum or a minimum.

definition: To differentiate u/v: (v times du/dx minus u times dv/dx) divided by v², where v is non-zero.
One function divided by another, such as (x² − 5)/(2x + 1).
The top of a fraction.
The bottom of a fraction.
The number e ≈ 2.718, the base for which the gradient of eˣ equals its value.
To differentiate a function of a function: derivative of the outside times derivative of the inside.
A function written with y as the subject, such as y = x³ − 2x.
A relation between x and y where y is not the subject, such as x³ + 5xy + y³ = 16.
Differentiating every term with respect to x, treating y as a function of x.
A straight line through a point on a curve with the same limiting gradient as the curve there.
The line perpendicular to the tangent at a point. For a finite, non-zero tangent gradient m, its gradient is −1/m; a horizontal tangent has a vertical normal.
Wrong: the derivative of uv is not du/dx × dv/dx.
Wrong order u dv/dx − v du/dx changes the sign of the answer.
Wrong: differentiating y² as 2y instead of 2y dy/dx when y is a function of x.
The graph of a quadratic function y = ax² + bx + c with a not zero. It is a symmetrical U-shaped curve: a valley (minimum) if a is positive and a hill (maximum) if a is negative.

The vertical line about which a parabola is symmetric. For y = ax² + bx + c its equation is x = −b/(2a). It passes through the turning point, and if there are two x-intercepts it is midway between them.

The minimum or maximum point of a parabola, which lies on the axis of symmetry. Its x-coordinate is −b/(2a); its y-coordinate is found by substituting that x into the equation of the curve. (This course does not use differentiation here.)
The point where a graph meets the y-axis. For y = ax² + bx + c it is the point (0, c).
The points where a graph meets the x-axis. For a quadratic they are the roots of ax² + bx + c = 0, if those roots are real.
The graph of a reciprocal function such as y = a/x (a not zero). Its typical shape is a hyperbola with two branches, and the axes are asymptotes.
The two-branched curve obtained as the graph of y = a/x (a not zero). The branches are mirror images; they never meet the axes.

A line that a graph approaches but does not meet. For y = a/x the asymptotes are the coordinate axes; for y = a/x + q they are the y-axis (x = 0) and the horizontal line y = q. The graph of y = tan x has vertical asymptotes at odd multiples of 90 degrees, or of π/2 radians.
One of the two separate parts of a hyperbola y = a/x. The branches are not joined across the asymptotes.

For the quadratic ax² + bx + c = 0, the quantity b² − 4ac. After a line is substituted into a circle, a positive discriminant means two intersection points, a zero discriminant means the line is a tangent (a repeated root), and a negative discriminant means no real intersection.
A quadratic equation with a repeated real root (discriminant zero) has two equal roots. In this section that means the line touches the circle at exactly one point and is a tangent.
The line that cuts a segment in half at right angles. The perpendicular bisector of a chord of a circle always passes through the centre of the circle.
The length of an arc of a circle of radius r that subtends an angle θ radians at the centre is rθ. The angle must be in radians.
The shorter arc joining two points on a circle, corresponding to a central angle less than π radians.
The longer arc joining two points on a circle, corresponding to a central angle greater than π radians. If the minor angle is θ, the major arc has length r(2π − θ).
The region of a circle bounded by two radii and the arc between them (a ‘slice’ of the circle). The perimeter of a sector is 2r + rθ.
The total length of the boundary of a region. For a sector this is two radii plus the arc; for a plate made by removing a segment it is the chord plus the remaining (usually major) arc.
The area of a sector of radius r and angle θ radians is (1/2)r²θ. The angle must be in radians.
The region of a circle bounded by a chord and the arc joining its ends. The area of a minor segment is the area of the sector minus the area of the triangular portion: (1/2)r²θ − (1/2)r² sin θ.

In this section the area of a triangle with two sides r and included angle θ radians is (1/2)r² sin θ, or (1/2)ab sin C in radian mode. Keep unrounded values when a later part, such as a segment area, depends on this calculation.
Two events are independent if either can occur without being affected by the occurrence of the other. For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
The rule P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) for independent events, and its extension to more than two independent events.
A diagram of successive outcomes with a probability on each branch. For independent events, multiply along a path and add mutually exclusive paths.
A selection in which each chosen item is returned before the next is chosen, so the probabilities are unchanged and the selections are independent.
Mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities cannot be independent, because then P(A ∩ B) = 0 but P(A)P(B) > 0.
A probability that depends on additional information about an outcome or event, written P(A | B) and read as the probability of A given that B has occurred.
The words used to read the symbol | in a conditional probability P(A | B): the probability of A, given that B has occurred.

term: using the original total as the denominator
definition: A common mistake in a conditional probability is to divide by the size of the original sample space instead of by the number of outcomes in the given event.
match: using the original total as the denominator

definition: The value m of a continuous random variable X for which the area under the PDF to the left of m is 1/2. Also called the 50th percentile.
The rth percentile of a continuous random variable X is the value xr such that the area under the PDF to the left of xr is r/100.
The 25th percentile of a continuous random variable: the value q1 such that P(X < q1) = 1/4.
The 75th percentile of a continuous random variable: the value q3 such that P(X < q3) = 3/4.
The difference IQR = q3 − q1 between the upper and lower quartiles of a continuous random variable.

term: taking the midpoint of the interval as the median
definition: The median of a continuous random variable is not, in general, the midpoint of the interval on which the PDF is non-zero; it depends on the shape of the density.
match: taking the midpoint of the interval as the median

term: integrating the wrong piece of a piecewise PDF
definition: For a piecewise PDF, first find the area of each complete piece so that you know which piece contains the required percentile, then integrate only inside that piece.
match: integrating the wrong piece of a piecewise PDF

term: keeping a root outside the support
definition: If the equation for a percentile is a quadratic, keep only the root that lies in the support of the PDF.
match: keeping a root outside the support

term: forgetting to differentiate the inside of a logarithm
definition: The derivative of ln f(x) is f'(x)/f(x), not 1/f(x). The chain rule contributes the derivative of the argument.
match: forgetting to differentiate the inside of a logarithm

definition: The standard derivatives of sin x, cos x and tan x, and the corresponding integrals, hold only when the angle is measured in radians, unless a question says otherwise.
A third variable, often t, in terms of which both x and y are given.
A pair of equations that give x and y in terms of a parameter.
Finding dy/dx from dy/dt and dx/dt by the chain rule: dy/dx = (dy/dt) / (dx/dt), provided dx/dt is not zero.
The derivative dy/dx is not equal to dy/dt. You must divide dy/dt by dx/dt.

term: losing the minus sign when integrating sine
definition: Because the derivative of cos x is −sin x, the integral of sin x is −cos x + c, and the integral of sin(ax+b) is −(1/a) cos(ax+b) + c.
match: losing the minus sign when integrating sine

term: multiplying by a instead of dividing when integrating
definition: The reverse chain rule for sin(ax+b), cos(ax+b) and sec²(ax+b) divides by a, the coefficient of x; it does not multiply by a.
match: multiplying by a instead of dividing when integrating

definition: A root of an equation in x is a value of x that satisfies the equation. On the graph of y equal to the left-hand side, the roots of y=0 are the x-intercepts.
An equation that can be written in the form ax^2+bx+c=0 with a not zero. Its solutions may be read from the corresponding parabola.
Two or more equations that are to be satisfied by the same values of the unknowns. For a straight line and a curve, the solutions are the coordinates of the points where the graphs meet.
Replacing a variable by an equal expression from another equation. Substituting the expression for y from a line into a curve produces an equation in x only.

The graph of a cubic polynomial in x. With a positive coefficient of x^3 the curve comes from the bottom left and leaves towards the top right; with a negative coefficient the directions are reversed.
The graph of y=a^x for a positive constant a other than 1. Every such graph passes through (0,1), because a^0=1.
Two events are dependent when the occurrence of one affects the probability of the other, as in selections without replacement.

term: using a simple product when events are dependent
definition: A common mistake is to multiply the two ordinary probabilities P(A)P(B) after a selection without replacement, instead of using a conditional probability in the product.
match: using a simple product when events are dependent

definition: For any two events A and B, P(A and B)=P(A)P(B given A)=P(B)P(A given B). When the events are independent this reduces to the product of the two ordinary probabilities.
To integrate sin^2 x or cos^2 x, first rewrite using a double-angle identity: sin^2 x = (1/2)(1-cos 2x) and cos^2 x = (1/2)(1+cos 2x).

term: integrating sin squared x as a power
definition: A common mistake is to write the integral of sin^2 x as (1/3)sin^3 x, instead of first using the double-angle identity.
match: integrating sin squared x as a power

definition: An equation between trigonometric expressions that holds for every value of the angle for which both sides are defined, such as tan squared x = sec squared x minus 1. Identities are used to rewrite expressions, for example before solving an equation or integrating.
For a continuous random variable X with PDF f, the expectation (mean) is E(X), the integral of x f(x) over the interval where f is non-zero.
For a continuous random variable X, Var(X) = E(X squared) minus the square of E(X), where E(X squared) is the integral of x squared times f(x).

term: stopping at E(X squared) when finding the variance
definition: A common mistake is to give E(X^2) as the variance, instead of subtracting the square of the mean.
match: stopping at E(X squared) when finding the variance

definition: The metric system measures length, mass and capacity in units linked by powers of ten, such as kilometres, metres and centimetres.
A change from one unit to another, using a conversion factor. Multiply when moving to a smaller unit and divide when moving to a larger unit.
A standard used to measure a quantity, such as the metre for length or the litre for capacity.
A way of writing times using the 12 hours from 12 midnight to 12 noon (am) and the 12 hours from 12 noon to 12 midnight (pm).
A way of writing times as four-digit times from 00 00 (midnight) to 23 59. Afternoon times are written by adding 12 hours to the 12-hour clock hour after 12 noon.
A table of departure and arrival times for a service such as a bus or a train, usually written in the 24-hour clock.
The smallest value that a rounded measurement could have come from. It is found by subtracting half a unit of the given accuracy.
The greatest value that a rounded measurement could have come from. It is found by adding half a unit of the given accuracy.

The range of possible true values of a rounded measurement, from the lower bound up to the upper bound. It may be written with a strict or a closed inequality at the upper end, according to the question.
Rewriting a quadratic expression as a product of linear factors, so that a quadratic equation can be solved by setting each factor equal to zero.

Rewriting a quadratic expression so that the variable appears only inside a squared bracket, using the identities x squared plus 2dx equals (x+d) squared minus d squared, and the corresponding identity with a minus sign.

The formula x equals open parenthesis negative b plus or minus the square root of b squared minus 4ac close parenthesis, all divided by 2a, which gives the roots of the quadratic equation ax squared plus bx plus c equals 0 when a is not zero.
Data described in words rather than numbers, also called categorical data, such as a colour or a blood type.
Data that take numerical values. Quantitative data are either discrete or continuous.
Numerical data that can take only certain separate values, usually from a count, and cannot be made more precise.
Numerical data that are measurements given to a chosen degree of accuracy and can, in principle, take any value in an interval.
A common mistake is to treat shoe size as a continuous measurement. Shoe size takes only certain separate values, so it is discrete, even though a size need not be a whole number.

A table for a small set of discrete data in which the last digit of each value is a leaf, attached to the earlier digits, which form the stem. The leaves on each row are written in order, and a key with units must be given.
A stem-and-leaf diagram with a shared stem and a set of leaves on each side, used to compare two data sets of the same kind.
The leading digits shared by the values in a row of a stem-and-leaf diagram, written in a vertical list of equal class widths.
The final digit of a data value in a stem-and-leaf diagram. Each leaf stands for one observation and the leaves in a row are ordered, with the smallest nearest the stem.
A statement, with the unit, that shows how to read a stem and a leaf as a data value, for example 1 | 2 means 12 employees.

term: forgetting the key on a stem-and-leaf diagram
definition: A common mistake is to draw a tidy stem-and-leaf diagram but omit the key, so a reader cannot tell what each stem and leaf together represent.
match: forgetting the key on a stem-and-leaf diagram

definition: The function defined by |x|=x when x is greater than or equal to 0, and |x|=-x when x is less than 0. Its value is the magnitude of x and is never negative. It is also called the absolute value.

term: keeping a candidate that makes the other side negative
definition: When |f(x)| is set equal to a linear expression that is not itself a modulus, each candidate must be substituted back. A value that makes the right-hand side negative is not a solution, because a modulus is never negative.
match: keeping a candidate that makes the other side negative

definition: The point of a V-shaped graph y = |ax+b| where the graph meets the x-axis, namely the point (-b/a, 0) when a is not zero.

term: assuming that a straight line always meets a V-shape at two points
definition: A common mistake when solving |ax+b| = cx+d graphically is to assume there are always two intersections. One candidate can fail when the line lies below the x-axis, so a sketch or a substitution check is required.
match: assuming that a straight line always meets a V-shape at two points

definition: A procedure that asks whether an observed result could reasonably have happened by chance under a stated claim, or whether the chance of such a result is small enough to be called statistically significant. A test cannot prove a claim with certainty.
The claim under test, written H0. In this subsection it is a stated value of a binomial probability p, and the test asks whether the data are consistent with that value.
The competing claim, written H1. In this subsection the alternative is one-tailed: either p is less than the value in H0, or p is greater than that value, but not both.

The threshold, often 5% or 10%, used to decide whether an observed tail probability is small enough to reject H0. It must be compared with the calculated tail, or used to read a critical value, before a conclusion is written.

The set of values of the test statistic that lead to rejection of H0. It is also called the rejection region. In a one-tailed binomial test it is a tail of the form X is at most c, or X is at least c.
The set of values of the test statistic that do not lead to rejection of H0. It is the complement of the critical region.

The boundary value of the test statistic that marks the edge of the critical region. For a one-tailed binomial test it is the largest (or smallest) integer in that tail for which the tail probability is still no greater than the significance level.
The observed quantity on which the test is based. In this subsection it is usually the number of successes X, or a continuity-corrected z-value when a normal approximation is used.

term: writing H0 as the suspicion being tested
definition: A common mistake is to put the experimenter's suspicion into H0, or to write H1 in the opposite direction to the claim being tested. H0 is the existing value of p; H1 follows the direction of the suspicion.
match: writing H0 as the suspicion being tested

definition: A straight-line graph that relates two quantities, such as miles and kilometres. A value on one axis is read across or up to the line and then across or down to the other axis.
The number of units of one currency that are equal to one unit of another currency. Multiply by the rate when changing from the currency written as 1, and divide when changing the other way.
The system of money used in a country, such as dollars, pounds, euros or yen. Amounts in one currency are changed into another using an exchange rate.
A method for solving a pair of linear simultaneous equations by adding or subtracting multiples of the equations so that one unknown cancels, leaving an equation in the other unknown.

A diagram for grouped continuous data in which the area of each column is proportional to the class frequency. There are no gaps between columns unless a class has frequency zero, and the vertical axis is frequency density.
The height of a histogram column, equal to the class frequency divided by the class width. It measures frequency per unit of the horizontal variable.
The difference between the upper class boundary and the lower class boundary of a class. It is the width of the corresponding histogram column.

An end of a class interval after rounding has been allowed for. The lower and upper class boundaries of a class are used to find the class width and the class mid-value, and to place the column of a histogram.
The mean of the lower and upper class boundaries of a class. It is also called the midpoint of the class.
The range of values belonging to one class, from its lower class boundary to its upper class boundary.

term: using the frequency as the column height
definition: A common mistake, when the classes have unequal widths, is to take the frequency itself as the height of a histogram column. The height must be the frequency density, so that area is proportional to frequency.
match: using the frequency as the column height

term: taking the class width from the rounded labels
definition: A common mistake is to compute a class width from rounded class labels, for example treating 60–62 as width 2, instead of using the class boundaries 59.5 and 62.5.
match: taking the class width from the rounded labels

definition: The total frequency of all values less than a given value. For grouped data it is obtained by adding the class frequencies up to that value.
A graph of cumulative frequency against the upper class boundaries of grouped continuous data. The starting point, at the lowest lower class boundary, has cumulative frequency 0.
A cumulative frequency graph in which the plotted points are joined by straight-line segments. Estimates taken from the polygon match those taken from a histogram for the same grouped data.
A cumulative frequency graph in which the plotted points are joined by a smooth curve. Away from the plotted points, readings from a curve need not agree with readings from a polygon.

term: plotting cumulative frequencies at class mid-values
definition: A common mistake is to plot cumulative frequencies at class mid-values. The totals are known exactly only at the upper class boundaries, and mid-value plots would themselves be estimates.
match: plotting cumulative frequencies at class mid-values

definition: An inequality that involves one or more expressions of the form |ax+b|. It may be rewritten using |a| < b if and only if -b < a < b, or |a| > b if and only if a < -b or a > b, or, when two moduli are compared, by squaring both sides.

A value of x at which the two sides of a modulus inequality are equal. The solution is found by testing the sign of the inequality on each side of these values, or by reading the corresponding intersections on a graph.
An expression a_n x^n + ... + a_1 x + a_0, where n is a non-negative integer and a_n is not zero. The coefficients are constants and x is a variable.
The highest power of x that appears in the polynomial, after any zero coefficients have been ignored.
The coefficient of the highest power of x in a polynomial. It is not zero.
The term of a polynomial that does not involve x; the coefficient a_0.
The polynomial that is being divided.
The polynomial that is dividing the dividend.
The polynomial obtained by dividing one polynomial by another, before any remainder is written down.
What is left after one polynomial has been divided by another. Its degree is less than the degree of the divisor. If the remainder is 0, the divisor is a factor of the dividend.
The identity dividend = divisor × (quotient of a polynomial) + remainder, used to record the result of dividing one polynomial by another.
A common mistake in long division is to forget a placeholder 0x^k when a power is missing, and then to subtract from the wrong column.
A hypothesis test in which the alternative hypothesis has a direction, using < or >, and the critical region lies in a single tail of the distribution.

A hypothesis test in which the alternative hypothesis uses ≠, because the claim is only that the parameter is different from the value in H0. The significance level is shared between the two tails, usually equally, and the observed tail probability is compared with half of the significance level.
A statement comparing two linear expressions, such as 3x-4 < 11. Its solutions form a range of values, which can be shown on a number line.
A line on which numbers are marked in order. For an inequality, a filled circle includes the end-point and an open circle excludes it.
A set of points in the coordinate plane that satisfy one or more inequalities. The boundary line is solid if equality is included and broken if it is not.
Two or more inequalities that must all be satisfied at the same time. The required region is the overlap of the individual regions.
An inequality that involves a quadratic expression, such as x^2-7x+10<0. It is solved by finding the roots of the corresponding equation and reading a sketch of the parabola.
A diagram or table used to display a data set, chosen to match the type and quantity of the data, the audience and the purpose, without being misleading.

A bar chart treats classes as comparable categories, so it is misleading for continuous data grouped in classes of unequal width; a histogram, with area proportional to frequency, is appropriate instead.
match: using a bar chart for classes of unequal width

definition: If, for a polynomial P(x), P(c)=0, then x-c is a factor of P(x). More generally, if P(b/a)=0, then ax-b is a factor of P(x).

term: testing x=c for the factor x+c
definition: To test whether x+c is a factor, substitute x=-c, not x=c.
match: substituting x=c to test the factor x+c

definition: If a polynomial P(x) is divided by x-c, the remainder is P(c). If P(x) is divided by ax-b, the remainder is P(b/a).

term: substituting the wrong point for a remainder
definition: For a remainder when dividing by x+c, substitute x=-c, not x=c. For a divisor ax-b, substitute x=b/a, not x=a/b.
match: substituting the wrong point for a remainder

definition: The logarithm to base 10 of a positive number y is the power to which 10 must be raised to obtain y: if 10^x=y, then x=log_10 y. The same value is given by the calculator keys log or lg.

term: swapping the base and the index of a logarithm
definition: In logarithmic form the index stands alone and the base of 10^x is the base of the logarithm: 10^x=y is x=log_10 y, not y=log_10 x.
match: writing the base and the index the wrong way round

definition: A quantity or function in which the variable appears as an index, such as \(10^x\). The exponential \(10^x\) and the logarithm to base 10 are inverse functions.
A Type I error occurs when a true null hypothesis is rejected. Its probability is the probability of landing in the critical region when H0 is true, and is at most the significance level of the test.
A Type II error occurs when a false null hypothesis is accepted. Its probability can be calculated only when a particular value of the parameter under H1 is given.

A fraction whose numerator or denominator, or both, contains an algebraic expression. It is simplified by cancelling a common factor, and combined by using a common denominator or by multiplying by a reciprocal.
A function for which each output that appears comes from exactly one input. A horizontal line meets the graph at most once.
A function for which each input has one output, but an output may come from more than one input. The mapping x to x squared, for real x, is many-one.
The set of allowed input values of a function. It must be stated as part of the definition of the function.
The set of output values that a function actually takes, as the input runs through the domain. The coursebook also uses the word codomain for this set of outputs.
The function obtained by applying one function and then another. The notation fg(x) means that g acts on x first, and then f acts on the result.
The function that undoes a given one-one function f. It is written f to the minus one. The domain of the inverse is the range of f, and the range of the inverse is the domain of f.
A function that is equal to its own inverse, so that f and f to the minus one are the same mapping. For example, f(x)=1/x for x not 0 is self-inverse.
The value that occurs most often in a set of data. A list may have more than one mode, or no mode at all.
In grouped data, the class with the highest frequency density. In a histogram it is the class with the tallest column.

term: taking the highest frequency as the modal class
match: taking the class with the highest frequency as the modal class
definition: The modal class is the class with the highest frequency density, not necessarily the highest frequency, unless every class has the same width.
If y = a^x, then x = log_a y, provided that a > 0, a is not 1, and y > 0. The functions a^x and log_a x are inverses.
For a positive base a other than 1, log_a(xy) = log_a x + log_a y, log_a(x/y) = log_a x - log_a y, and log_a(x^m) = m log_a x.
log_a(xy) = log_a x + log_a y, provided the logarithms are defined. This is not the same as the addition of x and y inside a single logarithm.

term: writing log x + log y as log(x + y)
match: writing log x + log y as log(x + y)
definition: The multiplication law of logarithms combines a product, not a sum: log x + log y = log(xy).
A discrete distribution for the number of events that occur singly, at random and independently in a fixed interval. If X ~ Po(λ), then E(X) = Var(X) = λ and P(X = r) = e^{-λ} λ^r / r!.
The single parameter λ of a Poisson distribution, equal to both the mean and the variance.

term: using the original mean for a different interval
match: using the original mean for a different interval
definition: If events occur at a constant rate, the Poisson parameter is proportional to the length of the interval and must be scaled before it is used.
The sum of a set of data values divided by the number of values. For ungrouped data it is (Sigma x)/n, and for a frequency table it is (Sigma xf)/(Sigma f).
Values rewritten as x-b or ax-b to make a calculation simpler. The original mean is recovered by undoing the coding: add b, and if there is a multiplier, then divide by a.

term: taking the mean of the two means
match: taking the mean of the two means
definition: The mean of two combined sets is the total of all the values divided by the total number of values. Averaging the two separate means is correct only when the two sets have the same size.
An equation in which the unknown appears inside a logarithm, or as the base of a logarithm. After using the laws of logarithms, every candidate must be checked so that each logarithm is defined.

term: forgetting to check that each solution makes the logarithms defined
match: forgetting to check that each solution makes the logarithms defined
definition: A value that satisfies an equation obtained after using the laws of logarithms is not a solution of the original equation if it makes an argument zero or negative, or if it makes a variable base non-positive or equal to 1.
An equation in which the unknown appears in an index. If the powers cannot be written with the same base, take logarithms of both sides and use the power law, then collect the unknown.

An inequality in which the unknown appears in an index. Taking logarithms leaves the inequality symbol unchanged if the base is greater than 1, but the symbol must be reversed if the base is between 0 and 1, or if you divide by a negative logarithm.

term: forgetting to reverse the inequality when the logarithm is negative
match: forgetting to reverse the inequality when the logarithm is negative
definition: If you take logarithms and then divide by a negative value, such as log 0.5, the inequality symbol must be reversed. The same reversal is needed if the logarithm itself has a base between 0 and 1.
The use of a Poisson distribution with mean np in place of B(n,p), when n is large and p is small. As a guide, the approximation is used when n>50 and np<5.

term: using a Poisson approximation when n is not large or np is not moderate
match: using a Poisson approximation when n is not large or np is not moderate
definition: A Poisson approximation to B(n,p) is suitable when n is large and p is small, so that np is moderate. As a guide, n>50 and np<5. The approximation is not equally good for every pair (n,p) with the same product np.
A diagram in which every length is a fixed fraction of the corresponding real length. The scale may be written as a ratio such as 1 to 50000, or in words such as 1 cm to 10 m.
The ratio that compares a length on a map or scale drawing with the real length it represents. The two lengths must be in the same unit before the ratio is written in the form 1 to n.
The angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when an observer looks up at an object. It is always measured from the horizontal.
The angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when an observer looks down at an object. It is always measured from the horizontal.
A direction measured as an angle clockwise from north. Bearings are used to describe the direction from one position to another.
A bearing written with three digits. For example, a bearing of 40 degrees is written 040 degrees, so that it is clearly a bearing and not a two-digit angle.
The bearing of the starting point from the finishing point. It differs from the original bearing by 180 degrees: add 180 degrees, or subtract 180 degrees if adding would give 360 degrees or more.
The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle. Its length does not depend on which of the two acute angles is being used.
In a right-angled triangle, the side that faces a chosen acute angle and is not the hypotenuse.
In a right-angled triangle, the shorter side that meets a chosen acute angle. It is not the hypotenuse.
For an acute angle A in a right-angled triangle, the sine of A is the length of the opposite side divided by the length of the hypotenuse.
For an acute angle A in a right-angled triangle, the cosine of A is the length of the adjacent side divided by the length of the hypotenuse.

For an acute angle A in a right-angled triangle, tan A is the length of the opposite side divided by the length of the adjacent side. The value depends only on the size of A, not on the size of the triangle.

A shift of a graph that does not change its shape or orientation. The graph of y=f(x)+a is a translation of y=f(x) by the vector (0, a). The graph of y=f(x-a) is a translation of y=f(x) by the vector (a, 0). Combining these, y=f(x-a)+b is a translation by the vector (a, b).
The transformation that sends each point (x, y) to (x, minus y). The graph of y equals minus f(x) is a reflection of the graph of y equals f(x) in the x-axis.
The transformation that sends each point (x, y) to (minus x, y). The graph of y equals f of minus x is a reflection of the graph of y equals f(x) in the y-axis.
The exact value of sine, cosine or tangent of 0, 30, 45, 60 or 90 degrees, written as an integer, a fraction or a surd, rather than a rounded calculator decimal.

term: angle between a line and a plane
definition: The angle between a line from a point to the plane and the line joining the foot of the perpendicular from that point to the same point on the plane. In a right-angled triangle this is the angle between the sloping edge and its projection on the plane.
match: angle between a line and a plane

definition: The acute angle that has the same sine, or the same cosine, or the same tangent, in absolute value, as a given angle. For an angle x between 0 and 360 degrees the related angle is used with the signs in each quadrant to find all solutions.

A transformation that enlarges or reduces all distances from an invariant axis by a constant scale factor. The graph of y=a f(x) is a stretch of y=f(x) by scale factor a parallel to the y-axis, and the graph of y=f(ax) is a stretch of y=f(x) by scale factor 1/a parallel to the x-axis.
Two or more transformations of a graph applied in a stated order. The resulting equation is found by carrying out the corresponding replacements or multiplications in that same order.

The middle value when the observations are arranged in order. For an odd number of observations it is the middle one; for an even number it is the mid-point of the two middle values. On a cumulative frequency graph it is read at half the total frequency.

A rearranged relationship, often obtained by taking logarithms, that can be plotted as a straight line. For example, if y=A e^{px} then ln y = ln A + p x, so a graph of ln y against x has gradient p and intercept ln A.

term: normal approximation to the Poisson distribution
definition: When the Poisson parameter lambda is large, a Poisson variable may be approximated by a normal variable with mean lambda and variance lambda. A continuity correction is used because the Poisson distribution is discrete.
match: normal approximation to the Poisson distribution

definition: The adjustment used when a discrete distribution is approximated by a continuous one: P(X less than or equal to k) is replaced by P(Y less than k plus one half), and P(X less than k) is replaced by P(Y less than k minus one half).
In any triangle, a over sin A equals b over sin B equals c over sin C, where side a is opposite angle A, and similarly for the other two sides.
In any triangle, a squared equals b squared plus c squared minus 2bc cos A, where a is the side opposite angle A. The same pattern holds for the other two sides.

term: area of a triangle using sine
definition: The area of a triangle is one half times the product of two sides and the sine of the included angle: one half ab sin C, where C is the angle between sides a and b. In this IGCSE work the calculator is in degree mode.
match: area of a triangle using sine

definition: The distance between two points P(x1, y1) and Q(x2, y2) is the square root of (x2-x1) squared plus (y2-y1) squared.
The midpoint of the segment joining P(x1, y1) and Q(x2, y2) is the point whose coordinates are the averages of the corresponding coordinates of P and Q.

The number m in the equation y=mx+c; it measures the steepness of the line. Parallel lines have equal gradients. If two lines are perpendicular and one has gradient m, the other has gradient -1/m, so the product of the gradients is -1.
Lines that never meet. In the coordinate plane, two non-vertical lines are parallel when they have the same gradient.
Lines that meet at a right angle. If their gradients are m1 and m2, then m1 times m2 equals -1.
A non-vertical straight line may be written y=mx+c, where m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept, or in the point-gradient form y-y1=m(x-x1). A vertical line has equation x=b.
The reciprocal of sine: cosec θ equals 1 over sin θ, or hypotenuse over opposite in a right-angled triangle.
The reciprocal of cosine: sec θ equals 1 over cos θ, or hypotenuse over adjacent in a right-angled triangle. This is the trigonometric ratio, not a secant of a circle.
The reciprocal of tangent: cot θ equals 1 over tan θ, or cos θ over sin θ, or adjacent over opposite in a right-angled triangle.

The identities that expand sin(A±B), cos(A±B) and tan(A±B) in terms of the sine, cosine and tangent of A and of B. In particular, sin(A+B) is sin A cos B plus cos A sin B, and cos(A+B) is cos A cos B minus sin A sin B.
The numerical difference between the largest and smallest values in a set of data. For grouped data a least and a greatest possible range can be stated from the class boundaries.

term: interquartile range of a data set
definition: The numerical difference Q3 minus Q1 between the upper and lower quartiles of a data set. It is the range of the middle half of the ordered values.
match: interquartile range of this data set
interquartile range of a data set

term: lower quartile of a data set
definition: The first quartile Q1 of an ordered data set: the median of the lower half of the values, or, for grouped data, the value at the appropriate position in a cumulative frequency table or graph.
match: lower quartile of a data set

term: upper quartile of a data set
definition: The third quartile Q3 of an ordered data set: the median of the upper half of the values, or, for grouped data, the value at the appropriate position in a cumulative frequency table or graph.
match: upper quartile of a data set

definition: The value that is n percent of the way through an ordered data set. In particular, the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles of a data set are the lower quartile, the median and the upper quartile.
For a single random variable X and constants a and b, E(aX+b) equals a E(X)+b. The result does not require independence of two random variables.
For a single random variable X and constants a and b, Var(aX+b) equals a squared times Var(X). A constant shift does not change the variance.
Finding a length or an angle in a solid by first identifying a right-angled triangle in the figure and then using Pythagoras’ theorem or a sine, cosine or tangent ratio in that triangle.
Data that record two measurements for each item, so that the relationship between the two measurements can be studied.
A diagram that plots one measurement against another for each item in a bivariate data set.
A description of the trend on a scatter diagram: positive if the points tend to rise from left to right, negative if they tend to fall, and none if there is no such pattern.
A straight line drawn through the cloud of points on a scatter diagram to show the trend, used to estimate one measurement from the other within the range of the data.
The completed-square equation of a circle with centre (a, b) and radius r is (x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r^2. The expanded form is converted back to this by completing the square.
For n values, the variance is the mean of the squared deviations from the mean, equal to (Sigma x^2)/n minus the square of the mean. In this syllabus the divisor is n, or Sigma f for grouped data.

term: standard deviation of a data set
definition: The square root of the variance of a data set.
match: standard deviation of a data set

definition: The identities sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A, cos 2A = cos^2 A - sin^2 A = 2 cos^2 A - 1 = 1 - 2 sin^2 A, and tan 2A = 2 tan A / (1 - tan^2 A).

Writing a sin theta + b cos theta as R sin(theta +/- alpha), or a similar single-sine or single-cosine form, with R = sqrt(a^2+b^2) and tan alpha = b/a, where R > 0 and 0 deg < alpha < 90 deg when a and b are positive.
If X and Y are independent, E(aX+bY)=a E(X)+b E(Y) and Var(aX+bY)=a^2 Var(X)+b^2 Var(Y). The mean formula does not need independence.
If X is normal then aX+b is normal. If X and Y are independent and each is normal, then aX+bY is normal, with mean a E(X)+b E(Y) and variance a^2 Var(X)+b^2 Var(Y).
match: independent random variables X and Y have the distributions N

definition: If X ~ Po(lambda) and Y ~ Po(mu) are independent, then X+Y ~ Po(lambda+mu). The parameters must first refer to the same interval.
The straight line that just touches a curve at a given point and has the same direction as the curve there. Its gradient is taken as the gradient of the curve at that point.
At a point on a curve, the gradient of the tangent at that point. It can be estimated by drawing a tangent and calculating rise over run, or found exactly from the derived function.
The gradient function of y, written dy/dx. For a power of x, the derived function of x^n is n x^{n-1}. A sum is differentiated term by term.
Another name for the derived function dy/dx, or for its value at a particular point.
If a continuous function f takes values of opposite sign at the ends of an interval, then the equation f(x)=0 has a root in that interval.
A function whose graph has no breaks on the interval being considered. A change of sign then guarantees at least one root.
A formula of the form x_{n+1}=F(x_n), used to produce a sequence of approximations to a root of x=F(x).
One application of an iterative formula, taking the current approximation as the input and producing the next approximation as the output.
A diagram of y=x and y=F(x) in which the iteration x_{n+1}=F(x_n) appears as a spiral approaching the intersection.
A diagram of y=x and y=F(x) in which the iteration x_{n+1}=F(x_n) appears as a stepped path approaching the intersection.

A trigonometric value written using integers, fractions and surds, without a rounded calculator decimal. The exact values of sine, cosine and tangent at 30°, 45° and 60° come from two standard right-angled triangles.
An angle measured as a rotation of a line OP from the positive x-direction. Anticlockwise rotations are positive and clockwise rotations are negative.
One of the four regions into which the axes divide the plane. The angle θ is said to be in the quadrant in which the rotating line OP lies.
The acute angle that the rotating line OP makes with the x-axis. Also called the reference angle.
A reminder of the signs of the trigonometric ratios in the four quadrants, read anticlockwise from the fourth: Cosine positive, All positive, Sine positive, Tangent positive.

term: trigonometric ratio of a general angle
definition: If P is the point (x,y) on the rotating line and r is the positive length of OP, then sin θ = y/r, cos θ = x/r and tan θ = y/x.

Half the difference between the greatest and least values of a bounded wave. For y = a sin x and y = a cos x, with a positive, the amplitude is a. The graph of y = tan x is unbounded and has no amplitude.

The smallest positive interval after which a function repeats. The period of y = sin x and of y = cos x is 360 degrees, or 2π radians; the period of y = tan x is 180 degrees, or π radians. For y = sin(bx) the period is 360 degrees divided by b, or 2π/b radians.

A line that divides a two-dimensional shape into two parts that are mirror images of each other. A reflection in a line of symmetry leaves the shape looking the same. A square has four lines of symmetry; a rectangle that is not a square has two.

A shape has rotational symmetry about a point if it looks the same after a rotation of less than one full turn about that point. The number of times the shape looks the same in a full turn of 360 degrees, including the original position, is the order of rotational symmetry.

The number of times a shape looks the same in a full turn of 360 degrees about a centre, including the original position. A regular n-sided polygon has order n, and the smallest angle of rotation that maps it onto itself is 360 degrees divided by n. A shape with no rotational symmetry other than a full turn has order 1.
A plane that cuts a solid into two parts that are mirror images of each other. A cuboid with three different edge lengths has three planes of symmetry; a cube has nine.

The inverse of sine on a restricted domain, written sin to the power minus 1, or arcsin. It is defined for inputs from minus 1 to 1, and its principal values lie between minus 90 degrees and 90 degrees, or between minus π/2 and π/2 radians.

The inverse of cosine on a restricted domain, written cos to the power minus 1, or arccos. It is defined for inputs from minus 1 to 1, and its principal values lie between 0 degrees and 180 degrees, or between 0 and π radians.

The inverse of tangent on a restricted domain, written tan to the power minus 1, or arctan. It is defined for all real inputs, and its principal values lie strictly between minus 90 degrees and 90 degrees, or strictly between minus π/2 and π/2 radians.

The unique value chosen for an inverse trigonometric function from its restricted range. For example, the principal value of sin to the power minus 1 of one half is 30 degrees, not 150 degrees, even though both angles have the same sine.

A rational expression in which the degree of the numerator is at least the degree of the denominator. An improper algebraic fraction is first rewritten, by polynomial division, as a polynomial plus a proper fraction, before any decomposition into partial fractions.

The decomposition of a proper rational expression into a sum of simpler fractions whose denominators are the factors of the original denominator. Distinct linear factors, a repeated linear factor, and an irreducible quadratic factor each have their own standard form.

The expansion of (a + b) to the power n, or of (1 + x) to the power n, as a sum of terms with binomial coefficients. When n is a positive integer the expansion is finite. When n is not a positive integer, (1 + x) to the power n = 1 + n x + n(n−1)/2! x squared + ⋯ is an infinite series valid for the absolute value of x less than 1, and for (1 + a x) to the power n it is valid for the absolute value of a x less than 1.
A quadrilateral whose four vertices all lie on a single circle. Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180 degrees.
The angle formed at the centre of a circle by two radii standing on an arc. It is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc.
The angle at the circumference standing on a diameter of a circle. It is a right angle.
The segment of a circle on the other side of a chord from a tangent at one end of the chord. The angle between the tangent and the chord is equal to the angle in the alternate segment.

The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord. It bisects the chord. Conversely, the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord, and the perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre.

A line about which a solid looks the same after a rotation of less than one full turn. A right prism with a regular polygonal cross-section has an axis of rotational symmetry through the centres of the two end faces.
Chords of a circle that have the same length. Equal chords are equidistant from the centre, and chords that are equidistant from the centre are equal.
For a positive integer n, n factorial, written n!, is the product n × (n − 1) × ⋯ × 2 × 1. By definition 0! = 1.
An arrangement of objects in which the order matters. The number of permutations of r objects chosen from n different objects is n!/(n − r)!.
A selection of objects in which the order does not matter. The number of combinations of r objects chosen from n different objects is n!/(r!(n − r)!).

A triangular array of numbers in which each row starts and ends with 1 and every other number is the sum of the two numbers above it. Row n gives the coefficients in the expansion of (a + b) to the power n.
The number n!/(r!(n − r)!), written as n over r in brackets or as nCr. It is the coefficient of the term in b to the power r in the expansion of (a + b) to the power n.
A sequence in which each term is found by adding the same number, the common difference, to the previous term. The nth term is a + (n − 1)d.
The fixed number d that is added to each term of an arithmetic progression to give the next term.
A sequence in which each term is found by multiplying the previous term by the same non-zero number, the common ratio. The nth term is a r to the power n − 1.
The fixed number r by which each term of a geometric progression is multiplied to give the next term.

A graph of cumulative frequency against the upper class boundaries, starting at the lower boundary of the first class with cumulative frequency 0. The points are joined by a smooth curve or by straight lines.
The complete set of items or people that a statistical investigation is about, for example all the students in a school.
A part of a population that is selected so that information about the population can be found from it.
A survey that collects information from every member of the population.
A sample of size n chosen so that every possible sample of size n from the population has the same chance of being chosen; in particular every member has the same chance of being chosen.
A complete list of the members of the population, from which a sample is chosen.
A sampling method is biased if some members or groups of the population are more likely to be chosen than others, so that the sample is not representative of the population.
For a geometric progression with first term a and common ratio r, where r is between −1 and 1, the sum to infinity is the limit of the sum of the first n terms as n increases: a/(1 − r).
An infinite series is convergent if the sum of its first n terms approaches a fixed value as n increases. A geometric series is convergent when r is between −1 and 1.
A comparison of two or more quantities of the same kind, written with colons, such as 3 : 5. A ratio has no units.
A ratio is in simplest form when its parts are whole numbers with no common factor other than 1.
The ratio of a length on a map or scale drawing to the real length, written as 1 : n. One unit on the map represents n of the same units on the ground.
A comparison of two quantities of different kinds, giving the amount of the first quantity for one unit of the second, such as litres per minute or kilometres per hour.
The total distance travelled divided by the total time taken for a whole journey.
A graph of distance from a starting point against time. Its gradient is the speed.
A graph of speed against time. Its gradient is the acceleration and the area under it is the distance travelled.
The rate of change of speed: the change in speed divided by the time taken, measured for example in metres per second squared.
A negative acceleration: the rate at which an object slows down.
Two quantities are in direct proportion if their ratio is constant, so y = kx for a constant k. Doubling one doubles the other.
Two quantities are in inverse proportion if their product is constant, so y = k/x for a constant k. Doubling one halves the other.
A method for proportion problems in which the value for one unit is found first and then multiplied by the number of units needed.
The constant k in a proportion equation such as y = kx or y = k/x.
A method of integration in which the variable is changed, for example u = g(x), so that the integral becomes a standard one in u. For a definite integral the limits are changed as well.
The method of integration given by the integral of u dv/dx = uv − the integral of v du/dx. It comes from integrating the product rule.
A random variable that can take only particular separate values, usually whole numbers obtained by counting.
A list or table of all the possible values of a discrete random variable together with their probabilities, which add up to 1.
Selecting objects one after another without putting each one back, so the number of objects left goes down by 1 after each selection.
The expectation (mean) of a random variable: the long-run average value, E(X) = Σ x P(X = x) for a discrete random variable.

term: variance of a discrete random variable
definition: Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))², where E(X²) = Σ x² P(X = x). It measures the spread of X about its mean.
match: variance of a discrete random variable

definition: The distribution B(n, p) of the number of successes in n independent trials, each with the same probability p of success: P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 − p)^(n − r).
In a binomial or geometric model, the outcome of a trial that is being counted. The other outcome is called failure.
The mean of the values in a random sample. As a random variable it has mean μ and variance σ²/n.
For a large random sample from any population with mean μ and variance σ², the sample mean is approximately normally distributed with mean μ and variance σ²/n.
The standard deviation of the sample mean, σ/√n.
An estimate of a population parameter whose average over all possible samples equals the true value. The unbiased estimate of σ² divides by n − 1.
The variance σ² of the whole population. It is usually unknown and is estimated from a sample.
A statement that two expressions are equal, containing an unknown whose value can be found by solving.
A quantity whose value is not known yet, represented by a letter in an equation.
To find the value or values of the unknown that make an equation true.
A rule written with letters that shows how one quantity is related to others, such as v = u + at.
The letter on its own on one side of a formula, such as v in v = u + at.
A rule that gives exactly one output for each input, written for example f(x) = 2x + 3.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as a displacement, written as a column or with i, j and k.
The size or length of a vector: for ai + bj + ck it is √(a² + b² + c²).
Vectors that are scalar multiples of each other, so they have the same or opposite directions.
A vector of magnitude 1. The unit vector in the direction of v is v divided by |v|.
The vector from the origin O to a point; the position vector of A is written a or OA.
For a = a₁i + a₂j + a₃k and b = b₁i + b₂j + b₃k, a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ = |a||b|cos θ, a number.
Non-zero vectors at right angles to each other; their scalar product is zero.
The angle θ between two vectors that both point away from the same point, found from cos θ = a·b / (|a||b|).
An equation r = a + λb giving the position vector r of any point on the line through a in the direction b.
The vector b in the line equation r = a + λb, giving the direction of the line.
The point N on a line such that the line from a given point to N is perpendicular to the line; it is the point of the line closest to the given point.
Lines in three dimensions that are not parallel and do not intersect.
Lines that have a point in common.
The derivative dy/dx or f'(x), which gives the gradient of a curve at any value of x.
A straight line segment joining two points on a curve.
The result of differentiating a function twice, written d²y/dx² or f''(x).
A function f is increasing on an interval if f(x) gets larger as x increases; f'(x) is positive there.
A function f is decreasing on an interval if f(x) gets smaller as x increases; f'(x) is negative there.

The distribution of the number of independent trials, each with the same probability p of success, up to and including the first success. If X ~ Geo(p), then P(X = r) = (1 − p) to the power r − 1 times p, for r = 1, 2, 3, …, and E(X) = 1/p.
A continuous distribution whose probability density graph is a symmetrical bell-shaped curve centred on the mean μ. It is written N(μ, σ²), where σ² is the variance.
The normal distribution with mean 0 and variance 1, written Z ~ N(0, 1). Its cumulative probabilities Φ(z) = P(Z < z) are given in tables.
To change a value x of X ~ N(μ, σ²) into z = (x − μ)/σ, the corresponding value of the standard normal distribution.
An interval calculated from a sample that is expected to contain an unknown population parameter in a stated proportion of samples. For a population mean it is x̄ ± z σ/√n.
A transformation in which every point of the image is the same distance from a mirror line as the object point, on the opposite side. It is described by the equation of the mirror line.
A transformation that turns a shape about a fixed point, the centre of rotation. It is described by the centre, the angle and the direction.
A transformation that moves every point of a shape the same distance in the same direction. It is described by a column vector.

A transformation that multiplies every distance from a fixed centre by the same scale factor. A scale factor between 0 and 1 makes the image smaller, and a negative scale factor puts the image on the other side of the centre, upside down.
The number by which every length is multiplied in an enlargement.
The fixed point from which distances are multiplied by the scale factor in an enlargement. It is found where the lines joining corresponding points of the object and image meet.
A vector written as two numbers one above the other in brackets: the top number is the movement to the right and the bottom number the movement up.
An equation that contains a derivative, such as dy/dx. Solving it means finding a relationship between the variables without derivatives.
A method for solving dy/dx = f(x)g(y): rewrite it as the integral of 1/g(y) with respect to y equal to the integral of f(x) with respect to x, then integrate both sides.
The solution of a differential equation that contains an arbitrary constant of integration.
The solution of a differential equation found by using a given condition to fix the value of the constant of integration.
How fast a quantity changes with respect to another quantity, usually time; the rate of change of y with respect to t is dy/dt.
Rates of change of two quantities that are linked by a formula, so that the chain rule connects them, for example dV/dt = dV/dr × dr/dt.
A stationary point where the gradient changes from positive to negative; there d²y/dx² is negative or zero.
A stationary point where the gradient changes from negative to positive; there d²y/dx² is positive or zero.
The number of items expected to have a property: the total number multiplied by the probability that one item has it.
Using a normal distribution N(np, npq) to estimate binomial probabilities when n is large; it is suitable when np > 5 and nq > 5, and a continuity correction is needed.
The proportion of a sample that has a property, p̂ = x/n; it is used as an estimate of the population proportion.
The proportion p of the whole population that has a property; it is usually unknown and estimated from a sample.
Two or more events considered together, such as a result on a first spin followed by a result on a second spin.
Events where the outcome of one does not affect the probability of the other; then P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
One or more. P(at least one) = 1 − P(none), which is often the quickest method.
The set of all the elements being considered, shown by the rectangle in a Venn diagram and written ℰ.
A number of the form bi, where b is real and i² = −1.
A number of the form x + iy, where x and y are real and i² = −1.
For z = x + iy, the real part is Re(z) = x.
For z = x + iy, the imaginary part is Im(z) = y, a real number.
The conjugate of z = x + iy is z* = x − iy; z z* = x² + y² is real.
A diagram in which the complex number x + iy is shown as the point (x, y): the horizontal axis is the real axis and the vertical axis the imaginary axis.
For z = x + iy, |z| = √(x² + y²), the distance of the point representing z from the origin.
The angle arg z from the positive real axis to the line joining the origin to the point representing z, measured anticlockwise, with −π < arg z ≤ π.
The form z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), where r = |z| and θ = arg z.
The form z = r e^(iθ), where r = |z| and θ = arg z.
Two complex numbers x + iy and x − iy. The non-real roots of a polynomial equation with real coefficients occur in conjugate pairs.
A square root of a complex number w is a complex number z with z² = w; every non-zero complex number has two square roots, z and −z.
The set of all points that satisfy a given condition, such as |z − a| = r (a circle) or |z − a| = |z − b| (a perpendicular bisector).
The reverse process of differentiation: finding a function from its derivative.
The numbers a and b in a definite integral from a to b: the lower and the upper limit.
The area between a curve and the x-axis from x = a to x = b, found as the definite integral of y from a to b when the curve is above the axis.
The points where two graphs meet, found by solving their equations simultaneously.
A definite integral with an infinite limit, or whose integrand is undefined at a limit; it is found as a limit of ordinary definite integrals, if that limit exists.
The volume of the solid formed when a region is rotated through 360° about an axis: π times the integral of y² dx about the x-axis, or of x² dy about the y-axis.
A solid formed by rotating a region through 360° about an axis.
